learning.text:
A test’s accuracy on sick people is not your chance of being sick.

When you get a Test +, you don’t know whether you came from the sick group or the healthy group. Right now, out of 1,000 people, 500 have the flu (yielding 480 true catches) and 500 are healthy (yielding 20 false alarms). Your actual chance of having the flu is 480 out of all 500 positive tests (96%).

See the step-by-step Bayes proof →

Why a rare disease creates mostly false alarms. When flu is rare (10% sick), 900 of 1,000 people are healthy. A 4% false-alarm rate on 900 healthy people creates 36 false alarms, next to only 96 true catches, so Precision is 72.7%.

With the test cutoff and score separation fixed, changing the sick portion changes Precision while TPR and FPR stay fixed wherever both rates are defined.

Overall Accuracy & The False Security Trap
Why accuracy alone can be dangerously deceptive on rare events
Test Accuracy: (All correct results ÷ Total)
960 out of 1,000 cases correctly classified
96%
Accuracy

Accuracy measures how often the test gives the right answer: catching flu (480 TP) plus clearing healthy people (480 TN).

⚠️ The False Security Trap: When flu is rare (e.g. 10% sick), a broken test that says "Negative" to every single patient achieves an impressive 50% accuracy—while failing to catch a single sick person (TPR = 0%)!

Same top number (TP), different bottom group: why TPR ≠ Precision

Look at TPR and Precision below: both have the exact same top number (TP = sick people caught)! The only difference is who you divide by. TPR divides horizontally by all sick people (top row), while Precision divides vertically by all positive tests (left column, which mixes sick catches with healthy false alarms). Hover or tap any part of a fraction below to outline it above.

Why use F1? It penalizes tests that sacrifice one metric for the other: if either Precision or Recall is terrible, F1 is dragged down.
Important caveat: F1 ignores healthy people who tested negative (TN)—it only looks at catches and mistakes among positive results.

Bayes’ theorem in 3 natural steps: from 1,000 people to your chance of flu

The easiest way to understand Bayes’ theorem is with 1,000 people: first split them by how common flu is (p = 50%), next count how many from each row get a Test +, and finally take the sick share of all positive tests (P(flu | test +)).

Why the 1,000-person count formula equals Bayes’ formula

The vertical bar | means “given”. Because TP = 1,000 × TPR × p and FP = 1,000 × FPR × (1 − p), the population size 1,000 cancels out from top and bottom—turning expected counts into Bayes’ exact rate formula for P(flu | test +).

How Sick Portion Changes Gaussians & Precision–Recall (While ROC Stays Fixed)

Drag the Sick portion slider above: watch the green Actual flu Gaussian grow or shrink relative to the gray Actual no flu Gaussian. The ROC curve stays completely fixed, whereas the Precision–Recall curve bends dramatically because false alarms (red FP tail) overwhelm true catches when p is small!

🚨 1. Screening / Safety First
Missing flu lets illness spread to vulnerable people. Cutoff set to 80% to catch nearly every case.
⚖️ 2. Balanced (Equal Weight)
False alarms and missed cases are equally undesirable. Standard 50% cutoff.
🛡️ 3. Conservative / High Stakes
Unnecessary treatments or panic carry severe harm. Only positive when high confidence.
